headline: Your nervous system
body: Through the same receptor adrenaline uses.
punch: And knocking it out increases bone mass.

headline: This whole field
body: Estrogen, androgens, growth hormone, IGF-1, thyroid. Every framework for bone growth runs on the endocrine system.
punch: The sympathetic nervous system is a separate input nobody includes.

headline: Bone and cartilage cells
body: The same receptor class that responds to adrenaline and noradrenaline. Catecholamines act directly on these cells, not just on blood flow to them.
punch: Stress chemistry has a direct receptor in your skeleton.

headline: Delete that receptor
body: Mice lacking beta-2 adrenergic receptors — either systemically or specifically in osteoblasts — show increased bone mass.
punch: Removing a nervous system signal built more bone.

headline: It also touches
body: Catecholamines influence chondrocyte-to-osteoblast transdifferentiation — one of the four competing theories for how growth plates actually execute closure.
punch: A nervous system input sitting on top of a cell-fate decision.

headline: Which connects
body: Chronic stress, sleep, and stimulant medication all move catecholamine signalling. This is a plausible mechanism linking those to skeletal outcomes.
punch: Plausible mechanism. Not a demonstrated height effect.

headline: Why nobody covers this
body: It sits outside the hormone framework, so it doesn't appear in the literature people in this space read. It isn't hidden — it's in a different silo.
punch: The gaps in a field are usually where its categories are.

headline: Be clear on the limits
body: Mouse genetics and cell-level work. No human height outcome data. This is a mechanism worth knowing, not a lever worth pulling.
punch: Knowing a pathway exists is not knowing how to use it.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
